Trustworthiness/reputability\
What documentation is available for each source?\
For Cailin's source, NCES, provides Public-Use Data File User’s Manual, public-use data files, survey questionnaire, and codebook/record-layout documentation.\
For Tony's source, U.S. Department of Education, provides Survey User’s Guide, Data Analysis Cutting Tool User Guide, downloadable institutional data files, survey reporting instructions and definitions.
For Jack's data, Plain Campus, it provides A CSV file and the two government databases it draws from. No methodology document is listed.\
What information is missing, unclear, or not stated in each source?\
For Cailin's data, the information missing includes: the 2021-22 response rate and final sample size, the mail follow-up details, the file format (earlier years used fixed-format ASCII), and the incident definitions.\
For Tony's data, the missing information includes: whether OPE verifies submissions, file formats, the earliest year available, and release timing.
For Jack's data, missing data includes: how non-reporting campuses are handled, and enrollment definition.\
What limitations or data quality issues might come from how each source was collected?\
For Cailin's data, there was only one respondent per school, so information could be different due to record-keeping or recall.\
For Tony's data, these are self-reported counts. The counts could be inaccurate to make the school appear better on paper.\
For Jack's data, it is unstable for smaller campuses. The score only uses a single year, so a smaller campus may have more violent crimes instead of petty crime, and still be viewed as having a low crime rate.\
Degree of relevance to research question\
How do the collection methods affect what kinds of conclusions someone could make?\
For Cailin's data, you can describe how common certain incidents, policies, and programs are among public schools, and compare groups such as school level or how "urban" the school is.\
For Tony's data, you can conclude how many incidents an institution reported in each Clery category and location, and how that changed over time.\
You can conclude where a campus falls on reported on-campus offenses plus VAWA reports per 1,000 students, relative to other ranked campuses.\
In order to answer your research question, would you be employing any of the variables as proxies?\
Using enrollment  as population ignores commuter versus residential mix and time on campus. Reported crime counts for safety shows what’s directly measured is a report. Safety is inferred from it.\
If you could improve one source, what additional data would you add?\
For Cailin's dataset, provided by NCES, I would add a response/nonresponse rate on the dataset page, not just the manual.\
Ethical soundness\
What possible bias might be present in either source?\
For all datasets, there is respondent/reporting bias in the sense of self-reporting. 
What ethical concerns might be connected to either source? Scope What does one row, record, case, or entry represent in each source?\
An ethical concern in some data includes privacy and how it's related to smaller campuses. If one student committed a crime at a smaller school, that data could potentially re-identify the criminal or victim.\
What populations do each dataset represent?\
Plain Campus and CSS represent college campuses across the United States, and NCES reports/represents K-12 across the country.\
Which is more relevant to your research question? Why?\
CSS is most relevant to our research question because it separates each crime by a ranking/weighing system to emphasize the severity of a crime.\
What other claims could someone reasonably make using these sources?\
One could make claims about what offense categories are most common in certain areas, schools, etc. You could also make claims about how CSS counts relate to enrollment.\
